194	```
195	
196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340

results.content:
# Visual Companion Guide Browser-based visual brainstorming companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and options. ## When to Use Decide per-question, not per-session. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?** **Use the browser** when the content itself is visual: - **UI mockups** — wireframes, layouts, navigation structures, component designs - **Architecture diagrams** — system components, data flow, relationship maps - **Side-by-side visual comparisons** — comparing two layouts, two color schemes, two design directions - **Design polish** — when the question is about look and feel, spacing, visual hierarchy - **Spatial relationships** — state machines, flowcharts, entity relationships rendered as diagrams **Use the terminal** when the content is text or tabular: - **Requirements and scope questions** — "what does X mean?", "which features are in scope?" - **Conceptual A/B/C choices** — picking between approaches described in words - **Tradeoff lists** — pros/cons, comparison tables - **Technical decisions** — API design, data modeling, architectural approach selection - **Clarifying questions** — anything where the answer is words, not a visual preference A question *about* a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What kind of wizard do you want?" is conceptual — use the terminal. "Which of these wizard layouts feels right?" is visual — use the browser. ## How It Works The server watches a directory for HTML files and serves the newest one to the browser. You write HTML content to `screen_dir`, the user sees it in their browser and can click to select options. Selections are recorded to `state_dir/events` that you read on your next turn. **Content fragments vs full documents:** If your HTML file starts with `/.hyperpowers/brainstorm/` for the session directory. **Note:** Pass the project root as `--project-dir` so mockups persist in `.hyperpowers/brainstorm/` and survive server restarts. Without it, files go to `/tmp` and get cleaned up. Remind the user to add `.hyperpowers/` to `.gitignore` if it's not already there. **Launching the server by platform:** **Claude Code:** ```bash # Default mode works — the script backgrounds the server itself. scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open ``` On Windows, the script auto-detects and switches to foreground mode (which blocks the tool call). Use `run_in_background: true` on the Bash tool call so the server survives across conversation turns, then read `$STATE_DIR/server-info` on the next turn to get the URL and port. **Codex:** ```bash # Codex reaps background processes. The script auto-detects CODEX_CI and # switches to foreground mode. Run it normally — no extra flags needed. scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open ``` **Copilot CLI:** ```bash # Start it with Copilot CLI's non-blocking/background shell mechanism so the # server survives across turns. Keep --foreground so the harness, not the # script, owns backgrounding. The launcher is a .sh, so invoke it via bash # (on Windows, call Git Bash's bash.exe from the PowerShell tool). bash scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open --foreground ``` **Other environments:** The server must keep running in the background across conversation turns. If your environment reaps detached processes, use `--foreground` and launch the command with your platform's background execution mechanism. If the URL is unreachable from your browser (common in remote/containerized setups), bind a non-loopback host: ```bash scripts/start-server.sh \ --project-dir /path/to/project \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --url-host localhost ``` Use `--url-host` to control what hostname is printed in the returned URL JSON. ## The Loop 1. **Check server is alive**, then **write HTML** to a new file in `screen_dir`: - **Required: confirm the server is alive before referring to the URL or pushing a screen.** Check that `$STATE_DIR/server-info` exists and `$STATE_DIR/server-stopped` does not. If it has shut down, restart it with `start-server.sh` using the **same `--project-dir`** — it reuses the same port, so the user's open tab reconnects on its own (it shows a "paused" overlay while the server is down) and you don't need to send a new URL. The server auto-exits after 4 hours idle (configurable with `--idle-timeout-minutes`). - Use semantic filenames: `platform.html`, `visual-style.html`, `layout.html` - **Never reuse filenames** — each screen gets a fresh file - Use your file-creation tool — **never use cat/heredoc** (dumps noise into terminal) - Server automatically serves the newest file 2. **Tell user what to expect and end your turn:** - Remind them of the URL (every step, not just first) - Give a brief text summary of what's on screen (e.g., "Showing 3 layout options for the homepage") - Ask them to respond in the terminal: "Take a look and let me know what you think. Click to select an option if you'd like." 3. **On your next turn** — after the user responds in the terminal: - Read `$STATE_DIR/events` if it exists — this contains the user's browser interactions (clicks, selections) as JSON lines - Merge with the user's terminal text to get the full picture - The terminal message is the primary feedback; `state_dir/events` provides structured interaction data 4. **Iterate or advance** — if feedback changes current screen, write a new file (e.g., `layout-v2.html`). Only move to the next question when the current step is validated. 5. **Unload when returning to terminal** — when the next step doesn't need the browser (e.g., a clarifying question, a tradeoff discussion), push a waiting screen to clear the stale content: ```html

Continuing in terminal...

``` This prevents the user from staring at a resolved choice while the conversation has moved on. When the next visual question comes up, push a new content file as usual. 6. Repeat until done. ## Writing Content Fragments Write just the content that goes inside the page. The server wraps it in the frame template automatically (header, theme CSS, connection status, and all interactive infrastructure). **Minimal example:** ```html

Which layout works better?

Consider readability and visual hierarchy

A

Single Column

Clean, focused reading experience

B

Two Column

Sidebar navigation with main content

``` That's it. No ``, no CSS, no `

steps.message:
The token sheet goes in `public/tokens.css`. Here's the short design.

**What it does**
The filter bar sits above the table (layout A) and has three groups of controls:
- **Show:** a radio group with four options: All events, Failed sign-ins (Sign-in failed only), Security changes (Password changed, Two-factor enabled, Email change requested) and Custom. Picking a shortcut sets the checkboxes. Ticking a checkbox by hand switches the radio to Custom.
- **Event type:** a fieldset with nine checkboxes and a legend.
- **Date range:** two native date inputs, From and To, plus a presets Select (Last 7 days, Last 30 days, All 90 days). That follows the guideline that a date range means two pickers plus presets. Dates are whole days in the viewer's time zone, both ends included, and limited to the 90-day window. If From is later than To, an inline error appears and the filter isn't applied.

Below the bar are a "12 of 48 events" count in a polite live region and a "Clear filters" button. When nothing matches, the table body is replaced by an empty state ("No events match these filters") with the same clear button. Changing a control filters right away. It never navigates or submits, and nothing goes into the URL.

**No JS**
The filter bar markup ships with the `hidden` attribute, and the script removes it. With JS off, nobody sees controls that can't work. The table itself still needs JS to render. That problem existed before this change and I'm leaving it alone unless you want it fixed here.

**Files**
- `public/tokens.css` (new, about 40 lines): only the semantic tokens the page uses, with light theme values from the 01 tables.
- `public/activity.html`: links `tokens.css` and adds the bar markup with labels above controls, a fieldset and legend, sentence case and no periods on labels.
- `public/activity.css`: styles the bar using tokens only. It also covers the focus ring, 24px minimum targets and a single column at 320px. I won't rewrite the existing raw values, because that would be a separate change.
- `public/activity.js`: the filtering is a pure function that takes the events and a filter state and returns the matching events. The render code reuses it.

**Testing**
- I'll check the pure function with Node's built-in `node --test`. That adds no dependencies, only one test file.
- Then I'll run each scenario by hand in a real browser and tell you which browser and what I clicked: each shortcut, a single week, From later than To, a filter with no results, clear, keyboard only, and 320px width.

**Commits**
I'll make two commits and show you the full diff before each one:
- `chore: add semantic token sheet`
- `feat: filter account activity by type and date`

I expect about 250 lines in total. If it goes past 300, I'll stop and propose how to split it.

Is this good to go?

# 01 Foundations

These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
reference it.

Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and

# 03 Forms

How fields, labels, help, validation, and saving behave on every form in the
app. These rules apply field by field and to the save behavior of a form as a
whole.

## Labels and help

- Every field has a visible label. Placeholder text is never a label and never
  holds information the user needs after they start typing.
- Labels sit above their control, left-aligned, in `--type-label`. The gap from
  label to control is `--space-4`.
- Checkbox and switch labels sit to the right of the control, and the whole
  label is clickable.
- Hint text sits between the label and the control in `--type-body-sm` and
  `--text-secondary`, and the control references it with
  `aria-describedby`.
- Mark required fields with "(required)" after the label when most fields are
  optional, or mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most are required.
  Never rely on an asterisk alone.
- Keep labels to a noun phrase: "Display name", not "Enter your display name".

## Field sizing

Size the control to the value it will hold, not to the container. A five-digit
number in a full-width input reads as a bug.

| Field type | Control | Width token | Validation | Keyboard and input mode | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Person name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 80 characters | autocomplete=name | Do not split into first and last unless a downstream system requires it |
| Display name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 50 characters, trimmed | autocomplete=nickname | Shown to other users |
| Email address | TextInput type=email | `lg` | Syntax check on blur, existence check on save | inputmode=email, autocomplete=email | Changing it sends a confirmation email |
| Phone number | TextInput type=tel | `sm` | E.164 after normalization | inputmode=tel, autocomplete=tel | Show the normalized form after blur |
| URL | TextInput type=url | `lg` | Absolute http or https | inputmode=url | Prefix https:// when the user omits a scheme |
| Password | TextInput type=password | `md` | Policy from the auth service | autocomplete=new-password | Show and hide toggle as an IconButton |
| One-time code | TextInput | `xs` | 6 digits | inputmode=numeric, autocomplete=one-time-code | Paste fills every box |
| Search | TextInput type=search | `lg` | none | enterkeyhint=search | Clear button inside the field |
| Integer quantity | TextInput type=number | `xs` | Min and max from the API | inputmode=numeric | No spinner arrows |
| Duration in minutes | TextInput type=number | `xs` | 1 to 1440 | inputmode=numeric | Suffix "min" inside the field |
| Currency amount | TextInput | `sm` | Two decimals, locale aware | inputmode=decimal | Currency symbol as a prefix |
| Percentage | TextInput | `xs` | 0 to 100 | inputmode=decimal | Suffix "%" |
| Date | Date picker | `sm` | Valid calendar date | Typed entry allowed | Format from 04 Content |
| Date range | Two date pickers | `sm each` | Start before end | Typed entry allowed | Presets in a Select beside it |
| Time | TextInput | `xs` | 24-hour or 12-hour per locale | inputmode=numeric | Never a Select of every minute |
| Time zone | Select searchable | `lg` | IANA zone id | Type-ahead | Default to the browser zone; show the UTC offset in each option |
| Language | Select | `md` | Supported locale list | Type-ahead | Each option in its own language |
| Country | Select searchable | `md` | ISO 3166 list | Type-ahead | Put the detected country first |
| Theme or appearance | RadioGroup | `n/a` | One of the listed values | Arrow keys | Options: Light, Dark, Match system |
| Single on or off setting saved with the form | Checkbox | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Use Switch only when the change applies immediately |
| Single on or off setting applied immediately | Switch | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Never inside a form that has a Save button |
| Several independent options | Checkbox list | `n/a` | Optional minimum | Space toggles | Fieldset with a legend |
| One of two to five options | RadioGroup | `n/a` | Required unless a default is safe | Arrow keys | Show every option |
| One of six or more options | Select | `md` | Required unless a default is safe | Type-ahead | Group long lists |
| Long free text | Textarea | `full` | Max length from the API | none | Counter when a max exists |
| Secret value, shown once | Read-only field with copy button | `lg` | none | Copy with one click | Mask after the first view |
| Secret value, regenerable | Read-only field plus Button | `lg` | Confirm before regenerating | none | Regenerating revokes the old value |
| Avatar or image | File input with preview | `n/a` | Type and size from the API | none | Show the current image beside the control |
| Color | Swatch picker | `n/a` | One of the palette tokens | Arrow keys | Never free-form hex |
| Tags | Combobox with chips | `lg` | Max count from the API | Enter adds, Backspace removes | Suggest existing tags first |

## Validation

- Validate on blur for format, on save for anything that needs the server.
  Never validate on every keystroke; the exception is a counter that shows the
  remaining characters.
- An invalid field shows the invalid state from 02 Components and a message
  directly below the control, in `--danger-text`, starting with the field
  name.
- On a failed save, move focus to the first invalid field and show a Banner
  with tone `danger` at the top of the form listing every invalid field as a
  link to that field.
- Keep what the user typed. Never clear a field because it failed validation.

## Saving

- A form with a Save button saves every field at once. Show the button in its
  `loading` state while saving and keep it in place; do not move or resize it.
- Disable nothing while saving. If the user edits a field mid-save, the next
  save sends the new value.
- On success, show a Toast ("Settings saved") and keep the user where they
  were. Do not navigate away and do not scroll.
- When the form has unsaved changes and the user tries to leave, confirm with
  a Dialog: title "Discard unsaved changes?", actions "Keep editing" (primary)
  and "Discard" (quiet).
- Settings that take effect immediately use a Switch and never sit inside a
  form with a Save button. Mixing the two on one page is allowed only when the
  immediate settings are clearly separated from the saved ones.
- Secrets (API tokens, recovery codes) are never sent back to the server on
  save. They are read-only, shown masked after the first view, and changed only
  through their own regenerate action with a confirming Dialog.

| Shift+Tab | Previous field | Previous field | Previous field | Reverse order |
| Enter | Submits the form | No effect | Opens or selects | Submits from any text field |
| Space | Types a space | Toggles | Opens | No effect |
| Escape | Clears a search field | No effect | Closes the list | Closes an open Dialog |
| Arrow keys | Moves the caret | No effect | Moves through options | Moves within a RadioGroup |
| Home / End | Line start or end | No effect | First or last option | No effect |

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user asked: "The account activity page is one long table of events and nobody can find anything in it. Add a way to narrow it down." I followed hyperpowers:brainstorming on the bounded path. The clarifying questions and the visual companion are done, and the short design was presented. **The user explicitly approved: "Yes, looks good — go ahead."** Implementation is now in progress on branch `feature/activity-filters`.

   Approved design:
   - **Filter bar above the table** (layout A, chosen by the user over my recommended B). It is always visible and wraps to one column at 320px.
   - **Show radio group** (the RadioGroup guideline covers 2 to 5 options). It has a legend and four options:
     - All events
     - Failed sign-ins: selects only "Sign-in failed".
     - Security changes: selects Password changed, Two-factor enabled and Email change requested, as the user confirmed.
     - Custom
     
     Picking a shortcut sets the checkboxes. Ticking a checkbox by hand switches the radio to Custom.
   - **Event type fieldset** with a legend and nine checkboxes, one per fixed type: Sign-in, Sign-in failed, Sign-out, Session expired, Password changed, Two-factor enabled, Email change requested, Settings updated, API token used.
   - **Date range:**
     - From and To are native `type=date` inputs, plus a presets Select with Last 7 days, Last 30 days and All 90 days.
     - Days are whole days in the viewer's local time zone, with both ends included, limited to the 90-day window.
     - If From is later than To, show an inline error and don't apply the filter.
   - **Result count** ("12 of 48 events") in a polite live region, plus a "Clear filters" button.
   - **Empty state** "No events match these filters", using `--text-secondary` and `--space-13` padding, with a clear button.
   - Changing a control filters immediately. It never navigates or submits, and nothing goes into the URL.
   - The filter bar markup ships with the `hidden` attribute, and JS removes it, so users without JS never see controls that can't work.
   - The table is still rendered only by JS. That is a pre-existing issue and I'm leaving it alone unless asked.
   - I will not rewrite the existing raw values in `activity.css`.
   - Files:
     - `public/tokens.css` (new, about 40 lines): only the semantic tokens used, with light theme values from the 01 tables.
     - `public/activity.html`: link `tokens.css` and add the bar markup.
     - `public/activity.css`: bar styles using tokens only.
     - `public/activity.js`: a pure filter function `(events, state) -> matching events` that the render code reuses.
   - Testing:
     - Test the pure function with Node's built-in `node --test`. This adds no dependencies, only one test file.
     - Check by hand in a real browser and report which browser was used and what I clicked: each shortcut, a single week, From later than To, a filter with no results, clear, keyboard only, and 320px width.
   - Commits, with the full diff shown before each and no push:
     - `chore: add semantic token sheet`
     - `feat: filter account activity by type and date`
   - The estimate is about 250 lines. If it grows past 300, stop and propose a split.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Static pages under `public/`, with no framework.
   - The data is `window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS` in `public/activity-data.js`:
     - About 48 events, newest first.
     - Each event has the fields `when` (a UTC ISO string like `'2026-09-28T17:42Z'`), `type`, `device`, `location`, `ip` (masked, like `203.0.113.x`) and `detail`.
     - The window is 90 days with a cap of 500 events. The largest real account has 311.
   - There is no test suite and no `.gitignore` in the repo. The companion writes to `.hyperpowers/`, and I suggested adding that folder to `.gitignore`.
   - Guideline rules:
     - Focus ring: 2px `--border-focus` at a 2px offset on `:focus-visible`. Never use `outline:none`.
     - Labels sit above their controls in `--type-label`, with a `--space-4` gap.
     - Checkbox lists go in a fieldset with a legend. RadioGroup is for 2 to 5 options. Select is for 6 or more.
     - A date range is two pickers plus a presets Select.
     - Changing a field must never submit.
     - Status messages go in a polite live region.
     - Sentence case, no periods on labels, "sign in" terminology.
     - Tabular nums in tables, targets at least 24px, reflow at 320px.
     - The empty state uses `--text-secondary`.
   - Token values from 01-foundations, needed for `tokens.css` (light theme). The palette hex values are given below.
     - Surfaces:
       - `--surface-page`: slate-50 `#f7f8f9`

   - `public/activity.html`: h1 "Account activity", the intro paragraph, and `<table id="activity-table">` with the headers When, Event, Device, Location, IP, Details and an empty tbody. It loads `activity-data.js` and then `activity.js`, and links `activity.css`.

   - `public/activity.js`, current code:
     ```js
     // Renders every event as one table row, in API order.
     const tbody = document.querySelector('#activity-table tbody');
     for (const event of window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS) {
       const row = document.createElement('tr');
       for (const value of [new Date(event.when).toLocaleString(), event.type, event.device, event.location, event.ip, event.detail]) {
     ```

6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After a context compaction:** a re-attached copy of this skill can be cut short (Claude Code keeps its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps). Before resuming work after any compaction, Read this file in full, along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.

196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

1	# 04 Content and accessibility
2	
3	How the interface talks, and the accessibility bar every page clears before it
4	ships.
5	
6	## Voice
7	
8	Plain, direct, and calm. Write the way a helpful colleague would say it out
9	loud. Lead with what the user can do, not with what went wrong. Prefer short
10	sentences and common words; cut any word that does not change the meaning.
11	
12	- Address the user as "you". Refer to the product as "we" only in messages
13	  where we did something ("We sent a code to your email").
14	- Never blame the user. "That code has expired" rather than "You entered an
15	  expired code".
16	- No exclamation marks outside of genuinely celebratory moments, and there are
17	  very few of those in a settings page.
18	- No jargon the user did not introduce. "Sign in", not "authenticate".
19	
20	## Capitalization and punctuation
21	
22	- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
23	  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
24	- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
25	  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
26	- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
27	  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
28	- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
29	  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.
30	
31	## Terminology
32	
33	Use the preferred term; reviewers flag the avoided forms.
34	
35	| Preferred | Avoid | Notes |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| sign in | log in, login (as a verb), authenticate | "Sign-in" as a noun or adjective |
38	| sign out | log out, logout | "Sign-out" as a noun |
39	| sign up | register, create login | Only on the public site |
40	| account | profile (for account-level settings) | Profile means the public-facing identity |
41	| profile | account (for public-facing identity) | Display name and avatar live here |
42	| settings | preferences, options, configuration | One word for every settings surface |
43	| display name | username, handle, nickname | There are no usernames in this product |
44	| email address | e-mail, mail, email ID | "Email" alone is fine in a label |
45	| time zone | timezone, TZ | Two words |
46	| language | locale | Locale is an implementation term |
47	| theme | appearance mode, skin | Light, Dark, Match system |
48	| notifications | alerts, messages | Alerts are a different, admin-only feature |
49	| email notifications | email alerts | Matches the field label |
50	| push notifications | mobile alerts, device notifications | Only for the mobile app and browser push |
51	| weekly digest | weekly summary, newsletter | Not a marketing email |
52	| two-factor authentication | 2FA, MFA, two-step verification | "Two-factor auth" in tight labels |
53	| recovery codes | backup codes | Shown once at setup |
54	| session timeout | idle timeout, auto logout | Minutes of inactivity before sign-out |
55	| API token | API key, access token, secret | Shown once, then masked |
56	| regenerate | reset, rotate, refresh | For tokens and codes |
57	| delete | remove, erase | Delete is permanent; remove is for detaching |
58	| remove | delete (when nothing is destroyed) | Removing a member keeps their account |
59	| save | apply, submit, update | For forms with a Save button |
60	| cancel | abort, back | Leaves without saving |
61	| discard | throw away, lose | Only for unsaved changes |
62	| dialog | modal, popup | In documentation; never shown to users |
63	| banner | alert bar, notice | In documentation |
64	| toast | snackbar, notification | In documentation |
65	| required | mandatory, compulsory | "(required)" after a label |
66	| optional | not required | "(optional)" after a label |
67	| invalid | wrong, bad, incorrect | In documentation; messages describe the fix |
68	| expired | timed out | For codes and sessions |
69	| offline | disconnected, no connection | In messages |
70	| workspace | organization, team, tenant | The billing and membership unit |
71	| member | user (inside a workspace) | User is fine in documentation |
72	| owner | admin (for the billing owner) | Admins are a separate role |
73	| admin | administrator, superuser | Short form everywhere |
74	
75	## Formats
76	
77	| Value | Format | Example (en-US) | Notes |
78	|---|---|---|---|
79	| Date | Locale medium date | Sep 14, 2026 | Never numeric-only in the interface |
80	| Date and time | Locale medium date, short time | Sep 14, 2026, 3:05 PM | Show the time zone when it differs from the user's |
81	| Relative time | Rounded, past only | 5 minutes ago | Switch to an absolute date after 7 days |
82	| Duration | Largest two units | 1 hr 20 min | Never "80 minutes" |
83	| Number | Locale grouping | 12,480 | Tabular figures in tables |
84	| Percentage | Up to one decimal | 12.5% | No space before % in en-US |
85	| Currency | Locale currency format | $1,250.00 | Always two decimals |
86	| File size | Binary units, one decimal | 2.4 MB | Use MB, not MiB, in the interface |
87	| Time zone | Zone name with UTC offset | Pacific Time (UTC−07:00) | Use the minus sign, not a hyphen |
88	| Phone | National format when local, else E.164 | (555) 010-4477 | Store E.164 |

90	## Accessibility checklist
91	
92	Every page clears every row before it ships. "How to check" is what reviewers
93	actually do.
94	
95	| Criterion | Level | Requirement | How to check |
96	|---|---|---|---|
97	| 1.1.1 Non-text content | A | Every meaningful image and icon has a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden | Inspect alt and aria-hidden on every img and svg |
98	| 1.3.1 Info and relationships | A | Headings, lists, tables, labels, and fieldsets are real elements, not styled divs | Read the page with styles disabled |
99	| 1.3.2 Meaningful sequence | A | DOM order matches visual order | Tab through the page and watch the focus order |
100	| 1.3.3 Sensory characteristics | A | Instructions do not rely on shape, position, or color alone | Read every instruction out of context |
101	| 1.3.4 Orientation | AA | Works in portrait and landscape | Rotate a tablet emulator |
102	| 1.3.5 Identify input purpose | AA | Personal-data fields carry autocomplete tokens | Check against the field table in 03 Forms |
103	| 1.4.1 Use of color | A | Color is never the only way to convey state | View in grayscale |
104	| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | AA | 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text | Use only the approved pairs in 01 Foundations |
105	| 1.4.4 Resize text | AA | Usable at 200% browser zoom without loss | Zoom to 200% and complete the main task |
106	| 1.4.5 Images of text | AA | No text rendered as images | Search the page for text in img |
107	| 1.4.10 Reflow | AA | No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px wide | Set the viewport to 320px |
108	| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | AA | 3:1 for control borders and focus indicators | Check input borders and the focus ring |
109	| 1.4.12 Text spacing | AA | No clipping with increased letter, word, and line spacing | Apply the text-spacing bookmarklet |
110	| 1.4.13 Content on hover or focus | AA | Tooltips are dismissible, hoverable, and persistent | Hover, then move into the tooltip, then press Escape |
111	| 2.1.1 Keyboard | A | Every action is reachable and operable by keyboard | Unplug the mouse |
112	| 2.1.2 No keyboard trap | A | Focus can always leave a component | Tab into and out of every widget |
113	| 2.4.1 Bypass blocks | A | A skip link reaches the main content | Press Tab once on load |
114	| 2.4.2 Page titled | A | The document title names the page and the product | Check the browser tab |
115	| 2.4.3 Focus order | A | Focus moves in a logical order | Tab through and note every jump |
116	| 2.4.4 Link purpose | A | Link text makes sense out of context | List every link and read it alone |
117	| 2.4.6 Headings and labels | AA | Headings and labels describe their content | Read the heading outline alone |
118	| 2.4.7 Focus visible | AA | The focus ring is always visible | Tab through on every surface color |
119	| 2.4.11 Focus not obscured | AA | Sticky headers and footers never hide the focused element | Tab to fields near the sticky footer |
120	| 2.5.3 Label in name | A | The accessible name contains the visible label | Compare labels with the accessibility tree |
121	| 2.5.7 Dragging movements | AA | Anything draggable has a non-drag alternative | Try every drag interaction by keyboard |
122	| 2.5.8 Target size | AA | Targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS px | Measure IconButtons and checkboxes |
123	| 3.1.1 Language of page | A | The html element has a lang attribute | Inspect the root element |
124	| 3.2.1 On focus | A | Focus never triggers a change of context | Tab through every field |
125	| 3.2.2 On input | A | Changing a field never navigates or submits on its own | Change every select and radio |
126	| 3.3.1 Error identification | A | Errors are identified in text | Submit the form empty |
127	| 3.3.2 Labels or instructions | A | Every field has a label and needed instructions | Read the field table in 03 Forms |
128	| 3.3.3 Error suggestion | AA | Error messages say how to fix the problem | Compare against the message catalog |

331	## Screen reader support
332	
333	Test with VoiceOver on Safari and NVDA on Firefox before shipping. A page
334	passes when a screen reader user can complete its main task without sighted
335	help, hears every validation message when it appears, and hears the save
336	confirmation without losing their place.

1	# 01 Foundations
2	
3	These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
4	reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
5	sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
6	review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
7	reference it.
8	
9	Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
10	meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and
11	point at a palette token per theme. Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette
12	tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet.

1	# Handoff notes
2	
3	Picking this back up from the last session. These are my notes so you have the context; the standing rules in them still apply. I will bring today's task myself.
4	
5	## Where things stand
6	
7	- The account-area rework has three parts. Part 1 (the activity events API) is done and lives in the separate `account-api` service repo, which is out of scope here. Part 2 (regrouping the settings page) shipped last week from a different branch. Part 3 is the account activity page in this repo, `public/activity.html`. Whatever I bring today is about that page.
8	- Part 1 landed as `account-api` PR #231, merged at `4be17c0` after two review rounds. Deployed to staging Monday, to production Tuesday 15:20 UTC behind the `activity_v2` flag, which is at 100% now.
9	- Nothing from Part 1 needs changes on the page side except what is listed under "Contract the page relies on" below. Do not re-open the API decisions; they were argued out with the backend reviewers already.
10	- The page still renders from the inline copy in `public/activity-data.js`. Wiring it to the live endpoint is a follow-up, not part of today.
11	- Part 2 is closed. Its review threads are resolved and the settings page is not to be touched from this branch.
12	
13	## Standing rules (verbatim from me, still in force)
14	
15	- "Show me the full diff before any commit. Never push. Never force-push. Never rewrite history on a shared branch."
16	- "One change per commit, conventional prefixes. If a change needs two kinds of prefix it is two commits."
17	- "Do not touch `public/legacy/` or anything under `vendor/` even if it looks dead. Ops still serves the legacy pages to two enterprise tenants."
18	- "Keep every page readable with JavaScript disabled. Interactive extras may require JS; the content may not."
19	- "No new runtime dependencies. Dev dependencies need a one-line justification in the commit body."
20	- "If a test is flaky, say so and show me the run. Do not retry until green and call it fixed."
21	- "When you are unsure whether something is in scope, ask me before doing it, not after."
22	- "Status lines between steps, short. No emojis anywhere."
23	- "Do not paste secrets into chat, commits, or test fixtures. The API token values on the settings page are real in staging; use the placeholder `tok_test_000` anywhere you need one."
24	- "The reviewers are strict about the UI guidelines. A review comment about a raw hex value or a hard-coded px size costs a full review round, so check before you hand anything over."
25	- "Never show a full IP address anywhere in the UI, logs, or screenshots. The API already masks the last octet; do not try to recover it."
26	- "Times are stored in UTC and shown in the viewer's time zone. Never show a bare UTC time without saying so."
27	- "Do not add analytics, tracking pixels, or third-party scripts to any page, including for debugging. Legal reviews every outbound request."
28	- "Keep the diff small enough to review in one sitting. If it grows past about 300 lines, stop and tell me how you would split it."
29	- "Run the page in a real browser before you say it works, and tell me which browser and what you clicked."
30	- "Do not rename files or move them between directories unless the task is about that. Ops' nginx config points at exact paths."
31	- "Write commit bodies for the reviewer who was not in the room: what changed, why, and what you checked."
32	
33	## Decisions from Part 1 (for reference; settled)
34	
35	1. Events are retained for 90 days, then deleted server-side. The page never needs to page past 90 days.
36	2. One request returns every event in the window, newest first. The cap is 500 events per user; the largest real account has 311. The page may assume the whole window is already loaded.
37	3. Event times are UTC ISO 8601 strings. The page formats them in the viewer's time zone (standing rule above).
38	4. Event types are a fixed list of nine: Sign-in, Sign-in failed, Sign-out, Session expired, Password changed, Two-factor enabled, Email change requested, Settings updated, API token used. New types need a backend change and a new review; do not invent client-side types.
39	5. IP addresses arrive masked (`203.0.113.x`). The page shows them as they arrive.
40	6. Location is a city-level geo lookup and may be `Unknown`. It is approximate; the page must not present it as exact.
41	7. Failed sign-ins are included on purpose. Security asked for them to be easy to spot, because the only support tickets about this page so far were people trying to find a failed sign-in they did not recognize.
42	8. API token use is aggregated server-side to one event per token per hour, so a busy integration does not drown out everything else.
43	9. "Settings updated" events carry the list of changed field names in `detail`, never the values. The page shows the names as they arrive.
44	10. No CSV or other export from this page. Legal wants exports to go through the data-request process.
45	11. "Sign out everywhere" and session revocation belong to the security page, which does not exist yet. The activity page stays read-only.
46	12. Events are immutable. There is no delete, hide, or "mark as recognized" action, and none is planned.
47	
48	## Contract the page relies on
49	
50	- `GET /api/v1/activity` returns `{events: [...]}` with fields `when`, `type`, `device`, `location`, `ip`, `detail`, newest first. `public/activity-data.js` is an exact copy of a real (anonymized) response, so its shape is the contract.
51	- The endpoint answers 403 when the `activity_v2` flag is off for a tenant. The page does not handle that yet; it is on the follow-up list.
52	- Field names will not change in v1. A v2 endpoint is not planned.
53	
54	## Review history (so you know what the reviewers look for)
55	
56	- Round 1 on Part 1 raised 11 comments: 5 about naming, 3 about missing event types in the docs, 2 about logging PII, 1 about the retention job's failure alert.
57	- Round 2 raised 2 comments, both resolved.
58	- The settings regroup (Part 2) took two review rounds. Round 1 was entirely guideline findings: a raw hex value in a section divider, a 13px label size that is not on the type scale, a focus ring drawn with `outline: none` plus a box-shadow, and a section heading in title case where the content guideline wants sentence case. The reviewers quoted the guideline table rows line by line.
59	- The profile header change before that took three rounds, for the same kinds of findings. The reviewers said in round 3 that they would start rejecting UI changes that arrive without the guideline check done.
60	
61	## Follow-ups (not for today unless they fall out naturally)
62	
63	- Wire the page to the live endpoint and handle the 403 flag-off case.
64	- Add an empty state for accounts with no events in the window.
65	- Show the viewer's time zone next to the "When" column header.
66	- Decide with Security whether failed sign-ins from unrecognized devices should get a stronger visual treatment.
67	- Build the security page (session revocation, token rotation).
68	
69	## Environment notes
70	
71	- The static pages are served by the ops nginx config, not by anything in this repo. Opening the HTML files directly in a browser works for local checks.
72	- Branch for today is `feature/activity-filters`, cut from master after Part 2.
73	- There is no test suite in this repo; the checks are the guideline review and a manual browser pass.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

<system-reminder>
<tools-used-before-summary>AskUserQuestion, Bash, Read, Skill, Write</tools-used-before-summary>

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user asked: "The account activity page is one long table of events and nobody can find anything in it. Add a way to narrow it down." I am following hyperpowers:brainstorming on the bounded path. Clarifying questions and the visual companion step are finished. The user approved the short design in chat with "Yes, looks good — go ahead." Implementation is now under way on branch `feature/activity-filters`, following TDD, with no plan document.

   Approved design:
   - **Placement.** A filter bar sits above the table (layout A, which the user chose). It is always visible and wraps to one column at 320px.
   - **Show radio group.** A fieldset with legend "Show" and four options:
     - All events
     - Failed sign-ins: selects only "Sign-in failed".
     - Security changes: selects Password changed, Two-factor enabled, and Email change requested.
     - Custom
     
     Choosing a shortcut sets the checkboxes. Ticking a checkbox by hand switches the radio to Custom.
   - **Event type.** A fieldset with legend "Event type" and nine checkboxes, one per fixed type: Sign-in, Sign-in failed, Sign-out, Session expired, Password changed, Two-factor enabled, Email change requested, Settings updated, API token used.
   - **Date range.**
     - Native `type=date` inputs labeled From and To, plus a presets Select offering Last 7 days, Last 30 days, and All 90 days.
     - Whole days in the viewer's local time zone, both ends inclusive, limited to the 90-day window.
     - If From is later than To, show the inline error "The end date must be after the start date." This is the `date_order` message from the 03 catalog, used verbatim. Show it in `--danger-text`, set aria-invalid, and do not apply the filter.
   - **Result count.** Text such as "12 of 48 events" in a polite live region (`aria-live="polite"`, role status), plus a "Clear filters" button.
   - **Empty state.** "No events match these filters" in `--text-secondary` with `--space-13` padding, and a clear button.
   - **Behavior.**
     - Changes filter immediately. The bar never navigates or submits: no form submit, and Enter in a date field must not submit, so either use no `<form>` or prevent submit. The URL is not changed.
     - The filter bar markup ships with the `hidden` attribute, and JS removes it.
     - The table is still JS-rendered. That is a pre-existing issue and stays out of scope unless the user asks.
     - Do not rewrite the existing raw values in `activity.css`.
   - **Files.**
     - `public/tokens.css` (new): palette tokens plus only the semantic tokens that are used, with light theme values.
     - `public/activity.html`: link tokens.css and add the bar markup.
     - `public/activity.css`: bar styles that use tokens only.
     - `public/activity.js`: a pure filter function `(events, state) -> matching events` that the render code reuses.
   - **Testing.**
     - `node --test` with one test file and no dependencies.
     - A manual pass in a real browser, then report which browser and what I clicked: each shortcut, a single week, From later than To, no results, clear, keyboard only, and 320px width.
   - **Commits.** Show the full diff before each commit, and never push.
     - `chore: add semantic token sheet`
     - `feat: filter account activity by type and date`
   
   The estimate is about 250 lines. If it goes past 300, stop and propose a split.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Data.** Static pages with no framework. The data is `window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS` in `public/activity-data.js`: about 48 events, newest first. Fields:
     - `when`: UTC ISO, for example `'2026-09-28T17:42Z'`
     - `type`
     - `device`
     - `location`: may be "Unknown"
     - `ip`: masked, like `203.0.113.x`
     - `detail`
   - **Repo state.** There is no test suite, and package.json exists. There is no `.gitignore`. The companion writes to `.hyperpowers/`, so suggest the user add it to .gitignore.
   - **Token rules (01).** Page CSS uses only semantic tokens. Palette tokens such as `--color-slate-50` appear only in the token sheet.

7

20	</HARD-GATE>

Before resuming work after any compaction, Read this file in full, along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
